title: Does the frustration-to-attack drive cancel what social agents learn in groups?
question: AB found that, without hazards, learning barely pays among social peers (+0.3) and more than doubles the attack rate. The candidate it named (other-agent sensors potentiating attack) did not hold in a probe: learning lowered those weights. A second probe pointed instead at the frustration drive: accumulated negative reward-prediction error adds a tonic current to the attack neurons, and trained agents were more frustrated than untrained ones. This study switches the drive off (aggression_gain=0) for the whole group, during training and testing.
background: Same design as AB: fixed dynamics (substeps=32, reset_each_decision, normalize with normalize_to='innate'), 12 agents and 24 food, no hazards, all agents train together for 1500 ticks, agent 0 is tested frozen among its frozen peers on 8 held-out worlds against a fresh untrained group with the same config. Exploratory probes on spent AB seeds 870-876 (tools/probes/attack_weights_probe.py, frustration_probe.py; test worlds 9800-9803): (1) learning lowered the mean weight from the other-agent sensors to attack (-0.11) and moved weight from active sensors (food, other agents) to silent ones in every condition, solo included; (2) test-time frustration was 0.28 trained vs 0.15 untrained and stayed 0.26 when no agent had the drive (agent 0 then attacked 5.0 times), so being attacked did not explain it; (3) the learning gain was +3.5 with the drive on and +6.0 with it off for the whole group at test only, with large seed-to-seed spread (-5.0 to +13.8). These probes used the drive only at test, not during training. Interpretation rule, fixed in advance: the frustration drive explains the group failure if H48a and H48b are supported. H48c tests the proposed route (learning raises frustration). Seeds 3100-3111 and worlds 9900-9907 have never been run.

hypotheses.statement: Without the frustration drive, learning pays among social peers
Removing the frustration drive raises the learning gain among social peers
With the drive, learning raises test-time frustration among social peers
Removing the drive shrinks the rise in attack rate that learning causes
Without the drive, social peers' learning gain differs from non-social peers'
